title: Terrorist Targeting, Relative Capacity, and State Military Response
A Theory of Terrorist Targeting and State Military Response
text:
Separating Equilibrium
The informational mechanism is strongest when types have divergent targeting incentives. Define:
\[
\Delta c(\theta) = c_S(\theta) - c_C(\theta), \quad \text{with } \Delta c(L) > \Delta c(H).
\]
Let \(\Delta R(\theta, z)\) denote the net strategic advantage of attacking a security target rather than a civilian target, excluding operational costs. A high-capacity organization selects \(S\) when \(\Delta R(H, z) \ge \Delta c(H)\), while a low-capacity organization selects \(C\) when \(\Delta R(L, z) < \Delta c(L)\).
When both hold, a separating equilibrium emerges:
\[
j^*(H) = S \quad \text{and} \quad j^*(L) = C.
\]

title: A Theory of Terrorist Targeting and State Military Response
text:
Pooling Equilibrium
If low-capacity organizations can easily target security personnel, \(\Pr(S \mid L)\) becomes substantial. When target choice pools:
\[
j^*(H) = j^*(L) = S \implies \mu(S) = \pi.
\]
Observing \(S\) conveys zero new information about capacity.

title: A Theory of Terrorist Targeting and State Military Response
text:
Semi-Separating Behavior
Consider \(\sigma_H(S) = 1\) and \(\sigma_L(S) = x \in (0, 1)\):
\[
\mu(S) = \frac{\pi}{\pi + (1 - \pi) x}, \quad \text{with } \frac{\partial \mu(S)}{\partial x} < 0.
\]

Target Hardness and Informational Content
The effect of security targeting through the informational channel increases with the degree to which the target distinguishes high-capacity from low-capacity organizations.

title: A Theory of Terrorist Targeting and State Military Response
text:
Deterministic Escalation Condition
In a baseline deterministic setting, following an attack on target \(j \in \{C, S\}\), a government of regime \(z\) escalates to military action (\(M\)) if and only if accumulated beliefs cross the regime-target threshold:
\[
\pi(n_S, n_C) \ge \bar{\mu}_j^z.
\]
Because public accountability dominates in democracies (\(P_C^D > P_S^D\)) while coercive apparatus protection dominates in autocracies (\(P_S^A > P_C^A\)), the structural cutoffs rank symmetrically:
\[
\bar{\mu}_C^D < \bar{\mu}_S^D \quad \text{and} \quad \bar{\mu}_S^A < \bar{\mu}_C^A.
\]

title: A Theory of Terrorist Targeting and State Military Response
text:
Probabilistic Formulation under Stochastic Shocks
In empirical environments, the additional cost of military deployment \(\Delta K^z\) is subject to unobserved political, diplomatic, or budgetary shocks:
\[
\widetilde{\Delta K^z} = \Delta K^z + \varepsilon, \quad \varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2).
\]
The probability of observing military escalation given cumulative frequencies \((n_S, n_C)\) and immediate attack target \(j\) is:
\[
\Pr(M \mid n_S, n_C, j, z) = \Phi\left( \frac{\pi(n_S, n_C) - \bar{\mu}_j^z}{\sigma_\mu} \right),
\]
where \(\Phi(\cdot)\) denotes the standard normal cumulative distribution function and \(\sigma_\mu = \frac{\sigma}{\Delta D_H - \Delta D_L}\).

title: A Theory of Terrorist Targeting and State Military Response
text:
Numerical Calibration and Predicted Outcomes
To illustrate the theoretical predictions, consider a standard baseline parameterization:

Prior belief: \(\pi_0 = 0.20\) (\(\Omega_0 = 0.25\))
Target informativeness: \(LR_S = 2.50\), \(LR_C = 1.10\)
Shock dispersion: \(\sigma_\mu = 0.15\)
Escalation cutoffs:

Democracy: \(\bar{\mu}_C^D = 0.05\) (highly sensitive to civilian casualties), \(\bar{\mu}_S^D = 0.45\) (demands substantial evidence of threat to justify military deployment for security hits)
Autocracy: \(\bar{\mu}_S^A = 0.00\) (attacks on coercive forces pose an existential threat), \(\bar{\mu}_C^A = 0.35\) (moderate tolerance for civilian casualties)

title: Terrorist Targeting, Relative Capacity, and State Military Response
text:
Terrorist capacity
Consider a Bayesian game between a terrorist organization \(T\) and a government \(G\). The terrorist organization has privately known organizational capacity:
\[
\theta\in\{\theta_L,\theta_H\},
\qquad
0<\theta_L<\theta_H.
\]
The organization observes its own type, but the government does not. The government’s prior probability that it confronts a high-capacity organization is:
\[
\Pr(\theta=\theta_H)=\pi_0,
\qquad
0<\pi_0<1.
\]
High capacity may reflect personnel, recruitment networks, intelligence and reconnaissance, logistics, weapons access, command and control, evasion of state surveillance, and the ability to replace operatives and sustain attacks over time. The government need not observe these attributes separately. It instead infers \(\theta\) from the organization’s observable targeting behavior.

title: Terrorist Targeting, Relative Capacity, and State Military Response
text:
Government capacity
Let:
\[
g>0
\]
denote the government’s relevant counterterrorism capacity. This includes the capabilities of police, intelligence, judicial, border-control, and related internal-security institutions. The government knows its own capacity. For parsimony, \(g\) is also observable to the terrorist organization.
Government capacity matters because the security consequences of terrorist capacity depend on the state’s ability to contain the threat. The same terrorist organization constitutes a more serious relative threat to a state with weak police and intelligence institutions than to a state with extensive surveillance, investigative, and enforcement capabilities.

title: Terrorist Targeting, Relative Capacity, and State Military Response
text:
Targeting outcomes
During the period under observation, the terrorist campaign produces:
\[
\mathbf n=(n_C,n_S),
\]
where \(n_C\) is the frequency of attacks against civilian targets and \(n_S\) is the frequency of attacks against state security targets. Security targets include military personnel and facilities, police, intelligence agencies, and other coercive institutions.
These variables measure target-specific campaign intensity, not attack severity. One large attack and many smaller attacks may produce different values of \((n_C,n_S)\) even when their total casualties are similar.

title: Terrorist Targeting, Relative Capacity, and State Military Response
text:
Government response
After observing \(\mathbf n\), the government chooses:
\[
r\in\{P,M\},
\]
where \(P\) denotes intensified policing, intelligence, judicial, or other internal-security measures and \(M\) denotes mobilization or deployment of military forces. The model focuses on the choice between these two escalatory instruments and therefore takes as given that the government has already chosen to respond more forcefully than under the preexisting status quo.

title: Terrorist Targeting, Relative Capacity, and State Military Response
text:
Sequence of play
The sequence is:

Nature draws terrorist capacity \(\theta\).
The terrorist organization observes \(\theta\) and selects a targeting strategy.
Civilian and security attack frequencies \((n_C,n_S)\) are realized stochastically.
The government observes \((n_C,n_S)\) but not \(\theta\).
The government updates its belief about \(\theta\).
The government evaluates inferred terrorist capacity relative to government capacity \(g\).
The government chooses \(P\) or \(M\).

In compact form:
\[
\boxed{
\theta
\longrightarrow
(\lambda_C,\lambda_S)
\longrightarrow
(n_C,n_S)
\longrightarrow
\mu(n_C,n_S)
\longrightarrow
\widehat{\rho}(n_C,n_S,g)
\longrightarrow
r\in\{P,M\}.
}
\]

In democracies:

At relatively low civilian-target frequency, the government may retain intensified policing. Once civilian attacks generate enough pressure for \(Z^D\geq0\), the government transitions to military action:
\[
\boxed{
n_C\uparrow:
\qquad
P\longrightarrow M
\quad\text{relatively readily in democracies}.}
\]

title: Terrorist Targeting, Relative Capacity, and State Military Response
text:
Autocracy
Civilian attacks also increase political pressure in autocracies if \(\alpha_C^A>0\), but the increase is smaller because \(\alpha_C^A<\alpha_C^D\). Autocratic governments therefore remain with policing over a wider range of civilian attack frequencies and transition to military action only after civilian attacks become sufficiently frequent or when they are already near the military threshold:
\[
\boxed{
n_C\uparrow:
\qquad
P\text{ persists longer before }M
\quad\text{in autocracies}.}
\]






ImportantProposition 1: Civilian-target frequency



Holding security targeting, government capacity, and response costs constant, increasing civilian-target attack frequency raises the likelihood of military response in both regimes. The increase operates primarily through political pressure and is stronger in democracies:
\[
\frac{\partial Z^D}{\partial n_C}
>
\frac{\partial Z^A}{\partial n_C}>0.
\]

title: Terrorist Targeting, Relative Capacity, and State Military Response
text:
Democracy
In democracies, the direct political effect of security targeting is relatively modest because \(\alpha_S^D<\alpha_C^D\). Nevertheless, repeated security attacks cause the government to revise upward its estimate of terrorist capacity:
\[
n_S\uparrow
\Rightarrow
\mu(n_C,n_S)\uparrow
\Rightarrow
\widehat{\rho}(n_C,n_S,g)\uparrow
\Rightarrow
Z^D\uparrow.
\]
At low security-target frequency, the government may rely on policing. As security targeting supplies greater evidence of a capable adversary, the government eventually crosses the military threshold:
\[
\boxed{
n_S\uparrow:
\qquad
P\longrightarrow M
\quad\text{in democracies through relative-threat updating}.}
\]
This transition can occur even when \(n_C=0\). A democratic government therefore does not require civilian victimization before employing military force.

title: Terrorist Targeting, Relative Capacity, and State Military Response
text:
Autocracy
In autocracies, security targeting produces the same informational effect, but it also generates stronger political pressure because \(\alpha_S^A>\alpha_S^D\). Increasing \(n_S\) therefore raises both inferred relative threat and regime-survival pressure:
\[
n_S\uparrow
\Rightarrow
\begin{cases}
\widehat{\rho}(n_C,n_S,g)\uparrow,\\
P^A(n_C,n_S)\uparrow\uparrow.
\end{cases}
\]
Both mechanisms raise \(Z^A\), causing an autocratic government to cross from policing to military action relatively readily:
\[
\boxed{
n_S\uparrow:
\qquad
P\longrightarrow M
\quad\text{relatively rapidly in autocracies}.}
\]






ImportantProposition 2: Security-target frequency



Holding civilian targeting, government capacity, and response costs constant, increasing security-target attack frequency raises the likelihood of military response in both democracies and autocracies:
\[
\frac{\partial Z^D}{\partial n_S}>0,
\qquad
\frac{\partial Z^A}{\partial n_S}>0.
\]
In democracies, the distinctive mechanism is upward revision of inferred terrorist capacity. In autocracies, the informational mechanism combines with political pressure to defend coercive institutions.








ImportantProposition 3: Autocratic security amplification



If \(\alpha_S^A>\alpha_S^D\) and the informational content of security targeting is the same across regimes, then:
\[
\frac{\partial Z^A}{\partial n_S}
>
\frac{\partial Z^D}{\partial n_S}.
\]
Security targeting therefore pushes autocratic governments toward military action more rapidly, provided the regimes have comparable government capacity, military costs, and response effectiveness.

title: Terrorist Targeting, Relative Capacity, and State Military Response
text:
Democratic civilian-targeting effect
Increasing civilian-target attack frequency increases the probability that a democratic government transitions from policing to military response:
\[
\boxed{
\frac{\partial\Pr(M)}{\partial n_C}\bigg|_D>0.
}
\]
The principal mechanism is political accountability for civilian protection.

title: Terrorist Targeting, Relative Capacity, and State Military Response
text:
Democratic security-learning effect
Increasing security-target attack frequency increases the probability that a democratic government transitions from policing to military response:
\[
\boxed{
\frac{\partial\Pr(M)}{\partial n_S}\bigg|_D>0.
}
\]
This relationship can occur even when civilian-target attack frequency is zero. The principal mechanism is an increase in inferred terrorist capacity relative to government capacity.

title: Terrorist Targeting, Relative Capacity, and State Military Response
text:
Autocratic security-amplification effect
Increasing security-target attack frequency increases the probability that an autocratic government transitions from policing to military response:
\[
\boxed{
\frac{\partial\Pr(M)}{\partial n_S}\bigg|_A>0.
}
\]
The effect operates through both inferred relative capacity and direct pressure to defend institutions central to regime survival.

title: Terrorist Targeting, Relative Capacity, and State Military Response
text:
Government-capacity effect
The positive relationship between security-target attack frequency and military response weakens as government capacity increases:
\[
\boxed{
\frac{\partial^2 Z^z}{\partial n_S\partial g}<0.
}
\]
The same increase in security targeting should be more likely to move a lower-capacity government from \(P\) to \(M\) than a higher-capacity government, other things equal.

title: A Theory of Terrorist Targeting and State Military Response
text:
States do not respond uniformly to terrorism. Some terrorist campaigns remain primarily matters for police, intelligence agencies, and courts, while others lead governments to mobilize or deploy military forces. Why does terrorist violence sometimes lead governments to cross this threshold?
I argue that terrorist targeting affects state responses through two distinct mechanisms:

Political mechanism: Different targets threaten governments in different ways, and the political meaning of those targets varies systematically across regime types. In democracies, violence against civilians can create intense public pressure on elected leaders to demonstrate that they are protecting the population. In autocracies, attacks against the military, police, and other coercive institutions can be especially threatening because these institutions constitute the organizational foundation of regime survival.
Informational mechanism: Governments do not observe terrorist organizational capacity perfectly. Terrorist organizations, however, know more about their own capabilities. Target selection and attack performance can therefore provide governments with information about the adversary they face. Successfully and repeatedly attacking well-protected security targets may require intelligence, trained personnel, logistics, weapons, organizational coordination, and the ability to evade state security services. Such attacks can consequently cause governments to revise upward their assessment of a terrorist organization’s capabilities.

These mechanisms are analytically distinct. Regime type determines how much political pressure a particular target generates, while organizational behavior provides information about terrorist capacity. The latter mechanism need not be regime-specific. An attack on a difficult military target can signal organizational capability to a democracy as well as an autocracy.
The argument can therefore be summarized as:
\[
\text{Terrorist targeting} \longrightarrow \begin{pmatrix} \text{Regime-specific political pressure} \\ \text{Belief updating about terrorist capacity} \end{pmatrix} \longrightarrow \text{State response}
\]
This distinction generates an important implication: security targeting can induce military action even in democracies. Democracies need not experience civilian attacks before turning to military force. If attacks against security institutions reveal that a terrorist organization poses a sufficiently serious security threat, military escalation can become rational even when the direct political pressure generated by security attacks is relatively modest.
At the same time, security targeting may have an especially pronounced effect in autocracies because the same attack can operate through both mechanisms simultaneously: it can reveal terrorist capability while also directly threatening institutions central to regime survival.

\bar{\mu}_C^D < \bar{\mu}_S^D \quad \text{and} \quad \bar{\mu}_S^A < \bar{\mu}_C^A.
\]

title: A Theory of Terrorist Targeting and State Military Response
text:
Probabilistic Formulation under Stochastic Shocks
In empirical environments, the additional cost of military deployment \(\Delta K^z\) is subject to unobserved political, diplomatic, or budgetary shocks:
\[
\widetilde{\Delta K^z} = \Delta K^z + \varepsilon, \quad \varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2).
\]
The probability of observing military escalation given cumulative frequencies \((n_S, n_C)\) and immediate attack target \(j\) is:
\[
\Pr(M \mid n_S, n_C, j, z) = \Phi\left( \frac{\pi(n_S, n_C) - \bar{\mu}_j^z}{\sigma_\mu} \right),
\]
where \(\Phi(\cdot)\) denotes the standard normal cumulative distribution function and \(\sigma_\mu = \frac{\sigma}{\Delta D_H - \Delta D_L}\).

title: A Theory of Terrorist Targeting and State Military Response
text:
Numerical Calibration and Predicted Outcomes
To illustrate the theoretical predictions, consider a standard baseline parameterization:

Prior belief: \(\pi_0 = 0.20\) (\(\Omega_0 = 0.25\))
Target informativeness: \(LR_S = 2.50\), \(LR_C = 1.10\)
Shock dispersion: \(\sigma_\mu = 0.15\)
Escalation cutoffs:

Democracy: \(\bar{\mu}_C^D = 0.05\) (highly sensitive to civilian casualties), \(\bar{\mu}_S^D = 0.45\) (demands substantial evidence of threat to justify military deployment for security hits)
Autocracy: \(\bar{\mu}_S^A = 0.00\) (attacks on coercive forces pose an existential threat), \(\bar{\mu}_C^A = 0.35\) (moderate tolerance for civilian casualties)

title: Terrorist Targeting, Relative Capacity, and State Military Response
Terrorist Targeting, Relative Capacity, and State Military Response
text:
Terrorist capacity
Consider a Bayesian game between a terrorist organization \(T\) and a government \(G\). The terrorist organization has privately known organizational capacity:
\[
\theta\in\{\theta_L,\theta_H\},
\qquad
0<\theta_L<\theta_H.
\]
The organization observes its own type, but the government does not. The government’s prior probability that it confronts a high-capacity organization is:
\[
\Pr(\theta=\theta_H)=\pi_0,
\qquad
0<\pi_0<1.
\]
High capacity may reflect personnel, recruitment networks, intelligence and reconnaissance, logistics, weapons access, command and control, evasion of state surveillance, and the ability to replace operatives and sustain attacks over time. The government need not observe these attributes separately. It instead infers \(\theta\) from the organization’s observable targeting behavior.

title: Terrorist Targeting, Relative Capacity, and State Military Response
text:
Government capacity
Let:
\[
g>0
\]
denote the government’s relevant counterterrorism capacity. This includes the capabilities of police, intelligence, judicial, border-control, and related internal-security institutions. The government knows its own capacity. For parsimony, \(g\) is also observable to the terrorist organization.
Government capacity matters because the security consequences of terrorist capacity depend on the state’s ability to contain the threat. The same terrorist organization constitutes a more serious relative threat to a state with weak police and intelligence institutions than to a state with extensive surveillance, investigative, and enforcement capabilities.

title: Terrorist Targeting, Relative Capacity, and State Military Response
text:
Targeting outcomes
During the period under observation, the terrorist campaign produces:
\[
\mathbf n=(n_C,n_S),
\]
where \(n_C\) is the frequency of attacks against civilian targets and \(n_S\) is the frequency of attacks against state security targets. Security targets include military personnel and facilities, police, intelligence agencies, and other coercive institutions.
These variables measure target-specific campaign intensity, not attack severity. One large attack and many smaller attacks may produce different values of \((n_C,n_S)\) even when their total casualties are similar.

title: Terrorist Targeting, Relative Capacity, and State Military Response
text:
Government response
After observing \(\mathbf n\), the government chooses:
\[
r\in\{P,M\},
\]
where \(P\) denotes intensified policing, intelligence, judicial, or other internal-security measures and \(M\) denotes mobilization or deployment of military forces. The model focuses on the choice between these two escalatory instruments and therefore takes as given that the government has already chosen to respond more forcefully than under the preexisting status quo.

title: Terrorist Targeting, Relative Capacity, and State Military Response
text:
Sequence of play
The sequence is:

Nature draws terrorist capacity \(\theta\).
The terrorist organization observes \(\theta\) and selects a targeting strategy.
Civilian and security attack frequencies \((n_C,n_S)\) are realized stochastically.
The government observes \((n_C,n_S)\) but not \(\theta\).
The government updates its belief about \(\theta\).
The government evaluates inferred terrorist capacity relative to government capacity \(g\).
The government chooses \(P\) or \(M\).

In compact form:
\[
\boxed{
\theta
\longrightarrow
(\lambda_C,\lambda_S)
\longrightarrow
(n_C,n_S)
\longrightarrow
\mu(n_C,n_S)
\longrightarrow
\widehat{\rho}(n_C,n_S,g)
\longrightarrow
r\in\{P,M\}.
}
\]

title: Terrorist Targeting, Relative Capacity, and State Military Response
Terrorist Targeting, Relative Capacity, and State Military Response
Terrorist Targeting, Relative Capacity, and State Military Response
Terrorist Targeting, Relative Capacity, and State Military Response
Terrorist Targeting, Relative Capacity, and State Military Response
Terrorist Targeting, Relative Capacity, and State Military Response
text:
Democracy
In democracies:
\[
n_C\uparrow
\Rightarrow
P^D(n_C,n_S)\uparrow
\Rightarrow
Z^D\uparrow.
\]
At relatively low civilian-target frequency, the government may retain intensified policing. Once civilian attacks generate enough pressure for \(Z^D\geq0\), the government transitions to military action:
\[
\boxed{
n_C\uparrow:
\qquad
P\longrightarrow M
\quad\text{relatively readily in democracies}.}
\]

title: Terrorist Targeting, Relative Capacity, and State Military Response
text:
Autocracy
Civilian attacks also increase political pressure in autocracies if \(\alpha_C^A>0\), but the increase is smaller because \(\alpha_C^A<\alpha_C^D\). Autocratic governments therefore remain with policing over a wider range of civilian attack frequencies and transition to military action only after civilian attacks become sufficiently frequent or when they are already near the military threshold:
\[
\boxed{
n_C\uparrow:
\qquad
P\text{ persists longer before }M
\quad\text{in autocracies}.}
\]






ImportantProposition 1: Civilian-target frequency



Holding security targeting, government capacity, and response costs constant, increasing civilian-target attack frequency raises the likelihood of military response in both regimes. The increase operates primarily through political pressure and is stronger in democracies:
\[
\frac{\partial Z^D}{\partial n_C}
>
\frac{\partial Z^A}{\partial n_C}>0.
\]

title: Terrorist Targeting, Relative Capacity, and State Military Response
text:
Democracy
In democracies, the direct political effect of security targeting is relatively modest because \(\alpha_S^D<\alpha_C^D\). Nevertheless, repeated security attacks cause the government to revise upward its estimate of terrorist capacity:
\[
n_S\uparrow
\Rightarrow
\mu(n_C,n_S)\uparrow
\Rightarrow
\widehat{\rho}(n_C,n_S,g)\uparrow
\Rightarrow
Z^D\uparrow.
\]
At low security-target frequency, the government may rely on policing. As security targeting supplies greater evidence of a capable adversary, the government eventually crosses the military threshold:
\[
\boxed{
n_S\uparrow:
\qquad
P\longrightarrow M
\quad\text{in democracies through relative-threat updating}.}
\]
This transition can occur even when \(n_C=0\). A democratic government therefore does not require civilian victimization before employing military force.

title: Terrorist Targeting, Relative Capacity, and State Military Response
text:
Autocracy
In autocracies, security targeting produces the same informational effect, but it also generates stronger political pressure because \(\alpha_S^A>\alpha_S^D\). Increasing \(n_S\) therefore raises both inferred relative threat and regime-survival pressure:
\[
n_S\uparrow
\Rightarrow
\begin{cases}
\widehat{\rho}(n_C,n_S,g)\uparrow,\\
P^A(n_C,n_S)\uparrow\uparrow.
\end{cases}
\]
Both mechanisms raise \(Z^A\), causing an autocratic government to cross from policing to military action relatively readily:
\[
\boxed{
n_S\uparrow:
\qquad
P\longrightarrow M
\quad\text{relatively rapidly in autocracies}.}
\]






ImportantProposition 2: Security-target frequency



Holding civilian targeting, government capacity, and response costs constant, increasing security-target attack frequency raises the likelihood of military response in both democracies and autocracies:
\[
\frac{\partial Z^D}{\partial n_S}>0,
\qquad
\frac{\partial Z^A}{\partial n_S}>0.
\]
In democracies, the distinctive mechanism is upward revision of inferred terrorist capacity. In autocracies, the informational mechanism combines with political pressure to defend coercive institutions.








ImportantProposition 3: Autocratic security amplification



If \(\alpha_S^A>\alpha_S^D\) and the informational content of security targeting is the same across regimes, then:
\[
\frac{\partial Z^A}{\partial n_S}
>
\frac{\partial Z^D}{\partial n_S}.
\]
Security targeting therefore pushes autocratic governments toward military action more rapidly, provided the regimes have comparable government capacity, military costs, and response effectiveness.

title: Terrorist Targeting, Relative Capacity, and State Military Response
text:
Democratic civilian-targeting effect
Increasing civilian-target attack frequency increases the probability that a democratic government transitions from policing to military response:
\[
\boxed{
\frac{\partial\Pr(M)}{\partial n_C}\bigg|_D>0.
}
\]
The principal mechanism is political accountability for civilian protection.

title: Terrorist Targeting, Relative Capacity, and State Military Response
text:
Democratic security-learning effect
Increasing security-target attack frequency increases the probability that a democratic government transitions from policing to military response:
\[
\boxed{
\frac{\partial\Pr(M)}{\partial n_S}\bigg|_D>0.
}
\]
This relationship can occur even when civilian-target attack frequency is zero. The principal mechanism is an increase in inferred terrorist capacity relative to government capacity.

title: Terrorist Targeting, Relative Capacity, and State Military Response
text:
Autocratic security-amplification effect
Increasing security-target attack frequency increases the probability that an autocratic government transitions from policing to military response:
\[
\boxed{
\frac{\partial\Pr(M)}{\partial n_S}\bigg|_A>0.
}
\]
The effect operates through both inferred relative capacity and direct pressure to defend institutions central to regime survival.

title: Terrorist Targeting, Relative Capacity, and State Military Response
text:
Government-capacity effect
The positive relationship between security-target attack frequency and military response weakens as government capacity increases:
\[
\boxed{
\frac{\partial^2 Z^z}{\partial n_S\partial g}<0.
}
\]
The same increase in security targeting should be more likely to move a lower-capacity government from \(P\) to \(M\) than a higher-capacity government, other things equal.
